/THURSDAY THROUGH MONDAY/...
Issued at 225 PM MDT Mon Sep 7 2026

Ensemble guidance continues to be supportive of ridging moving in 
overhead at 500-mb Thursday morning. This would be producing a 
surface high pressure across the Midwest. At the same time, there 
looks to be a surface low to the north across South-Central Canada 
and portions of the Northern United States. Weak southerly winds 
would be favored across the forecast area by this pattern. High 
temperatures are currently in the mid to upper 80s, and possibly 
lower 90s. Temperatures would be allowed to reach into the mid and 
upper 90s if southerly flow were stronger, but the current forecast 
would suggest that the surface high in the Midwest and the surface 
low to the north will be too far north to have a significant impact 
on southerly flow. Additionally, there are not any major mid level 
features that would promote strong winds mixing down to the surface, 
suggesting that highs may be a bit cooler than in recent weeks. As 
for precipitation, showers may be lingering across portions of 
Northwest Kansas and far East-Central Colorado in association with 
convection from the previous night. Otherwise, precipitation is not 
expected the rest of the day Thursday. 

A surface low is favored to form across the Northern and Central 
Plains in the right entrance region of a modest 50-70 kt 500-mb jet 
streak Friday. A cold front looks to be trailing the surface 
low as a surface high intrudes into the Northern United States. 
Southerly flow is anticipated out ahead of the surface low, 
though it is currently uncertain how soon the cold front will 
pass over the forecast region. LREF standard deviation in wind 
direction highlights this point, as a broad area from the 
Dakotas down through the South-Central High Plains shows a 
spread of 70-90 degrees in wind direction. Additionally, there 
is some uncertainty in how strong the cold front will be. 
Forecast highs Friday are currently in the low to mid 90s, 
though about 10-20% of NBM solutions show a faster, stronger 
cold front which would prevent highs from reaching the 90s. Dry 
conditions are also forecast across our Eastern Colorado 
Counties, where winds are primarily expected out of the west to 
northwest. LREF guidance shows a 30-50% chance across this area 
that relative humidity (RH) values drop below 20%. This may 
implicate fire weather as a concern, especially if stronger 
winds are experienced with the cold front Friday. NBM guidance 
across Western Yuma County shows around a 1 in 3 chance that 
wind gusts will reach 25 mph or higher. Confidence in Red Flag 
conditions being met (25 mph or greater gusts, and 15% or less 
RH for 3 hours) is less than 5%, although this will continue to 
be a point to watch as we approach the weekend. 

By Saturday, another trough is favored to be digging into the 
Western United States, moving eastward toward the forecast region 
through the weekend. A surface low at the leading edge is forecast 
to move into the Central Rockies Saturday, allowing southerly winds 
to return to the forecast area. Even so, highs only have about a 30-
40% chance on Saturday, and a 40-50% chance on Sunday to reach back 
into the 90s. This could certainly depend on how cool things can 
drop with Friday's cold front, but the surface winds also have an 
easterly component as opposed to a westerly component, which would 
prevent the hotter solution. There is the possibility for some 
precipitation on Saturday ahead of the low, but NBM guidance 
suggests that most areas have less than a 20% chance of receiving 
greater than 0.1 inches of precipitation. These chances increase a 
bit on Sunday into the 25-40% range as the low moves into Eastern 
Colorado and Wyoming. These higher probabilities are primarily 
across Southwest Nebraska and Northern Yuma County in Colorado, 
where a warm front may reside. However, some storms may develop 
ahead of an incoming cold front as well. Some storms may be allowed 
to become severe, as LREF guidance shows up to a 75% chance that 
sfc-500mb shear will be above 30 kts. Even so, the same 
guidance shows that it is most likely (>80%) that storms will 
only have a few hundred J/kg of surface CAPE (a measure of 
atmospheric instability) at their disposal. Therefore, the 
favored solution is that showers and weak thunderstorms would 
occur, with a storm or two that could become marginally severe. 

The cold front from this system is currently forecast to pass 
through the area sometime Sunday evening or overnight. There are
